arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Ronald Eisenberg represented the sides that brought the case. He detailed the extensive mitigation evidence presented at trial. He emphasized the jury instruction requiring unanimity to reject evidence.
Mr. Flora represented the opposing sides. He cited Lockett and Eddings as foundational precedents. He argued that barriers to full consideration of mitigating evidence are impermissible.
Chief Justice Rehnquist closed the argument. He stated the case was submitted for decision.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case concerns a jury instruction given during a 1983 murder trial. The instruction told jurors they must consider mitigating evidence unless they unanimously rejected it. The defense argues this rule prevents full consideration of the defendant's background. The state argues the instruction was legally sound.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The defense wants the Court to strike down the jury instruction. They argue it unconstitutionally blocks full consideration of mitigating evidence.
The state wants the Court to uphold the jury instruction. They argue the instruction did not violate constitutional requirements.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The defense argues that Lockett and Eddings require full consideration of mitigating evidence. They claim a unanimity requirement creates an unconstitutional barrier.
The state argues the instruction allowed the jury to consider all evidence. They contend the requirement did not preclude full effect of the evidence.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This dispute defines how juries must weigh a defendant's background. It determines whether unanimity requirements can limit the impact of mitigating evidence. The outcome shapes sentencing procedures in capital cases nationwide.
